articleTitle: On the potential for computer vision in undergraduate group projects
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: Computer vision offers an exciting opportunity to combine wide-based and challenging group project work within an advanced technical programme; this is the approach adopted within the 4-year MEng in Information Engineering. In the fourth year, students study subjects in small groups with coordinated coursework material. Image processing and computer vision is one of the five options and includes image formation; image transforms and coding restoration; and feature extraction. Coursework initially centred on a selection of short (mainly software) assignments to enable students to appreciate limitations and benefits of particular vision techniques. This was replaced by more demanding exercises requiring teamwork to achieve a video-rate image processing system. Two such projects are described and evaluated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital image processing and machine vision-an educational support package
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: This paper describes an integrated package developed for teaching purposes. In this context the package has been designed with the pre-requisite of accessibility in mind such that the student may experiment with both the hardware and software components. The student is able to gain a tacit knowledge of the image processing techniques and the package provides a platform for related coursework and final year projects. The complete system is IBM PC compatible and comprises a CCD camera, a digitising and storage card, a monitor and the source/executable code for the various image processing, feature extraction and classification algorithms.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: This paper is based on ten years' experience of teaching Applied Machine Vision in Graduate Diploma and M.Sc. courses in Information Technology and Mechatronics. The content and methodology of a modular course are described in relation to constraints on time and other resources. Operation of a system based on the Acorn BBC computer is outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The teaching of applied image processing at the University of Brighton
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: In 1987/88 the undergraduate courses in Electrical and Electronic Engineering were fundamentally redesigned in response to the changing needs of industry. The aim was to produce a thoroughly modern and relevant course which presented the discipline from a 'top-down' perspective. It also featured fully integrated Engineering Applications and commercial awareness and a learning environment where the establishment of rigid subject boundaries is actively discouraged. Another prime requirement was that graduates should be able to work competently in teams and communicate effectively at all levels with their peers. A programme of phased, integrative assignments runs through the first two years of the course, providing the core study of the discipline. Each assignment is supported, rather than pre-empted, by relevant lecture material and laboratory supervision by a teaching team. The cohesiveness of the whole course is maintained by an extensive monitoring and management infrastructure.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Teaching digital image processing within a general engineering course
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: The aims of the course are formulated within the described constraints; to awaken some awareness and enthusiasm for a previously unfamiliar subject; to provide all students with the image processing skills and techniques deemed desirable, irrespective of their choices of previously taken modules; and to cater for the different expectations of Mechanical, Electrical/Electronic and 'General' Engineers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The life and death of LIPS: some lessons from the design and use of courseware for teaching digital image processing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: This paper describes the development, use, and demise of a suite of computer programs, data, and student workbooks. Eight lessons for future courseware developers are adduced from this experience.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: This paper describes the methods employed to introduce students to image analysis and processing techniques at both the Undergraduate and the Graduate Level. A taught Undergraduate Course in Geographical Information Systems largely tackles problems of classification on existing images rather than the acquisition and processing of such images. The author draws on other examples taken from experience particularly in Soil Micromorphology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Implications of teaching image processing without reference to computer vision
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: Two modules each lasting one semester, and running consecutively, are described in outline. The Image Processing module proceeds from local and global spatial domain techniques, convolution and Fourier transforms, to filtering and other frequency domain techniques. The Computer Vision module deals with binary image geometry and topology and pattern recognition (extended to neural nets). It is argued that combining the two into a single course could improve the learning experience.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital image processing in undergraduate courses
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: Facilities available to students consist of a network of SUN, HP-Apollo and PC compatibles all running the HIPS image processing package and available on open-access or booking. HIPS and in-house developed packages are also installed on a Concurrent Computer System 6600 and a Sparcstation-LX in a Digital Signal Processing Laboratory used for research and final year projects. DIP facilities provide an attractive means of capturing undergraduate student interest in the early years of the course. Computer and video demonstrations given to first year student seminar groups provide a focal point for discussing both the broad context of Digital Signal Processing and DIP application, and the detail of particular operations, many of which can be explained effectively in qualitative terms.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Approaches to the university teaching of image analysis and understanding
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Teaching of Digital Image Processing in Universities
abstract: The authors distinguish between an artificial intelligence style and an engineering style in computer vision teaching. They discuss the academic content of courses and the comparative roles of laboratory sessions and equipment in the two approaches.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
